deltoid: Lateral third of clavicle, acromion, spine of scapula
Abducts arm (15–90°); anterior fibres flex, posterior fibres extend
Surgical-neck fracture or shoulder dislocation can injure the axillary nerve: flat shoulder + numb "regimental badge" patch. Common IM injection site.
supraspinatus: Starts abduction (first 15°); holds humeral head in glenoid
Most commonly torn rotator cuff muscle; painful arc 60–120°; tested by the "empty can" test.
subscapularis: Medial rotation of arm; stabilises shoulder anteriorly
Only rotator cuff muscle on the front of the scapula; lift-off test.
teres minor: Upper part of lateral border of scapula
Lateral rotation of arm; rotator cuff
Weakness of lateral rotation and a numb badge patch point to axillary nerve injury.
pectoralis major: Clavicular head: medial half of clavicle. Sternocostal head: sternum and upper 6 costal cartilages
Adducts and medially rotates arm; clavicular head flexes
Absent in Poland syndrome. Forms the anterior axillary fold.
pectoralis minor: Landmark: axillary artery is divided into 3 parts by this muscle.
serratus anterior: Costal surface of medial border of scapula
Protracts scapula and rotates it upward (arm above 90°)
Long thoracic nerve injury (e.g. mastectomy, axillary surgery) causes a winged scapula.
latissimus dorsi: Spines of T7–L5 via thoracolumbar fascia, iliac crest, lower 3–4 ribs, inferior angle of scapula
Floor of intertubercular groove of humerus
Extends, adducts and medially rotates arm
Climbing and crutch-walking muscle; used in breast reconstruction flaps.
trapezius: Superior nuchal line, external occipital protuberance, nuchal ligament, spines of C7–T12
Lateral third of clavicle, acromion, spine of scapula
Accessory nerve injury in the posterior triangle gives a drooping shoulder and weak shrug.
sternocleidomastoid: Manubrium sterni and medial third of clavicle
Mastoid process and lateral superior nuchal line
Turns face to the opposite side; both together flex the neck
Congenital torticollis; divides the neck into anterior and posterior triangles.
biceps brachii: Long head: supraglenoid tubercle. Short head: tip of coracoid process
Flexes elbow, supinates forearm, weak shoulder flexion
Biceps reflex tests C5–6. Long head tendon ruptures give a "Popeye" bulge.
brachialis: Distal half of front of humerus
Coronoid process and tuberosity of ulna
Musculocutaneous nerve (plus a small radial part)
Main elbow flexor in all forearm positions
Lies deep to biceps; "workhorse" of elbow flexion.
coracobrachialis: Landmark for the musculocutaneous nerve and axillary artery.
triceps brachii: Long head: infraglenoid tubercle. Lateral head: above radial groove. Medial head: below radial groove
Extends elbow; long head also adducts/extends shoulder
Triceps reflex tests C7. Radial nerve runs in the spiral groove between the heads.
brachioradialis: Flexes elbow, best in mid-prone position
The only elbow flexor supplied by the radial nerve; reflex tests C5–6.
pronator teres: Humeral head: medial epicondyle. Ulnar head: coronoid process
Middle of lateral surface of radius
The median nerve passes between its two heads (pronator syndrome).
flexor carpi radialis: Tendon is the landmark for the radial pulse and the median nerve.
palmaris longus: Weak wrist flexion; tenses palmar fascia
Absent in about 14% of people; tendon is a common graft.
flexor carpi ulnaris: Humeral head: medial epicondyle. Ulnar head: olecranon and posterior ulna
Ulnar nerve lies deep to it at the wrist; tendon marks the ulnar artery.
flexor digitorum superficialis: Humero-ulnar head (medial epicondyle, coronoid) and radial head
Sides of middle phalanges of medial 4 fingers
Tests PIP flexion with the other fingers held extended.
flexor digitorum profundus: Proximal ¾ of ulna and interosseous membrane
Lateral half: median (anterior interosseous). Medial half: ulnar
Only muscle that flexes the DIP joint; "jersey finger" is rupture of its tendon.
supinator: Lateral epicondyle, supinator crest of ulna, radial collateral ligament
Upper third of radius (lateral, anterior, posterior)
Posterior interosseous nerve (deep branch of radial, C5–6)
Posterior interosseous nerve passes through it (arcade of Frohse).
extensor carpi radialis longus: Radial nerve palsy leaves wrist drop; this muscle is spared by posterior interosseous lesions.
extensor carpi radialis brevis: Origin is the site of tennis elbow (lateral epicondylitis).
extensor carpi ulnaris: Lateral epicondyle and posterior border of ulna
Works with flexor carpi ulnaris to adduct the wrist.
abductor pollicis longus: With extensor pollicis brevis forms the lateral border of the anatomical snuffbox; de Quervain tenosynovitis.
extensor pollicis brevis: Base of proximal phalanx of thumb
De Quervain tenosynovitis; positive Finkelstein test.
extensor pollicis longus: Base of distal phalanx of thumb
Winds around Lister's tubercle; can rupture after a distal radius (Colles) fracture.
abductor pollicis brevis: Lateral base of proximal phalanx of thumb
Thenar wasting in severe carpal tunnel syndrome.
opponens pollicis: Opposition is the movement that makes the human grip precise.
adductor pollicis: Oblique head: capitate and 2nd–3rd metacarpals. Transverse head: 3rd metacarpal
Medial base of proximal phalanx of thumb
Froment's sign: thumb IP flexes to grip paper when ulnar nerve is injured.
palmar interossei: Extensor expansions of the same fingers
PAD and DAB: Palmar ADduct, Dorsal ABduct.
dorsal interossei muscles of hand: Extensor expansions; bases of proximal phalanges
Abduct fingers (DAB); flex MCP, extend IP joints
Wasting between the metacarpals suggests ulnar nerve or T1 lesion.
lumbrical muscles of hand: Lateral two: median nerve. Medial two: ulnar nerve
Flex MCP joints, extend IP joints
Only muscles that originate from tendons and not bone; claw hand when the medial two are paralysed.
gluteus maximus: Posterior ilium behind posterior gluteal line, sacrum, coccyx, sacrotuberous ligament
Iliotibial tract and gluteal tuberosity of femur
Used in climbing stairs and rising from a chair; largest muscle in the body.
gluteus minimus: Outer ilium between anterior and inferior gluteal lines
Abducts and medially rotates hip; stabilises pelvis
Superior gluteal nerve injury gives a Trendelenburg gait (pelvis drops on the opposite side).
tensor fasciae latae: Anterior superior iliac spine and iliac crest
Iliotibial tract, then lateral tibial condyle
Tenses fascia lata; assists hip flexion and abduction
Iliotibial band friction syndrome in runners.
piriformis: Key landmark in the gluteal region; the sciatic nerve usually exits below it.
obturator internus: Inner surface of obturator membrane and bone
Tendon bends 90° around the lesser sciatic notch; forms part of the pelvic side wall.
obturator externus: Outer surface of obturator membrane and bone
Posterior division of the obturator nerve supplies it.
quadratus femoris: Medial circumflex femoral artery runs along its upper border.
iliacus: Part of iliopsoas, the chief hip flexor.
psoas major: Transverse processes and bodies of L1–L5 and T12
Psoas abscess from TB spine; pain on hip extension (psoas sign) in appendicitis.
sartorius: Flexes, abducts, laterally rotates hip; flexes knee
Longest muscle in the body (the tailor muscle); forms the lateral border of the femoral triangle.
rectus femoris: Anterior inferior iliac spine and above acetabulum
Patella via quadriceps tendon, then tibial tuberosity
Only quadriceps head crossing the hip; knee jerk tests L3–4.
vastus lateralis: Greater trochanter, lateral lip of linea aspera
Preferred IM injection site in infants.
vastus medialis: Intertrochanteric line and medial linea aspera
Extends knee; lowest fibres stop lateral patellar dislocation
vastus intermedius: Anterior and lateral shaft of femur
gracilis: Body and inferior ramus of pubis
Adducts thigh; flexes and medially rotates knee
Often used as a graft or free flap.
pectineus: Forms the floor of the femoral triangle (with iliopsoas).
adductor brevis: Body and inferior ramus of pubis
Lies between pectineus and adductor longus anteriorly.
biceps femoris: Long head: ischial tuberosity. Short head: linea aspera
Long head: tibial part of sciatic. Short head: common fibular part
Flexes knee; long head extends hip
Common fibular nerve lies behind its tendon: foot drop risk at the fibular neck. A hamstring.
soleus: Soleal line of tibia, head and upper shaft of fibula
Called the peripheral heart: pumps venous blood upward.
gastrocnemius: Ankle jerk tests S1–2; Thompson test checks the Achilles tendon.
plantaris: Long thin tendon; rupture can mimic a DVT (tennis leg).
popliteus: Posterior tibia above the soleal line
Unlocks the knee by laterally rotating the femur on the tibia (medial rotation of tibia)
tibialis anterior: Lateral surface of upper two-thirds of tibia
Medial cuneiform and base of 1st metatarsal
Weakness gives foot drop and a high-stepping gait.
tibialis posterior: Navicular tuberosity and other tarsal/metatarsal bones
Inverts and plantarflexes foot; supports medial arch
Tendon passes behind the medial malleolus; dysfunction causes acquired flat foot.
fibularis longus: Head and upper two-thirds of lateral fibula
Medial cuneiform and base of 1st metatarsal
Everts and weakly plantarflexes foot; supports arches
Superficial fibular nerve injury weakens eversion.
fibularis brevis: Avulsion fracture of the 5th metatarsal base after an inversion injury.
extensor digitorum longus: Anterior compartment syndrome threatens deep fibular nerve.
flexor hallucis longus: Base of distal phalanx of great toe
Flexes great toe; supports medial arch
Tendon grooves the posterior talus and sustentaculum tali.
flexor digitorum longus: Bases of distal phalanges of lateral 4 toes
Tom, Dick And Very Nervous Harry: order behind the medial malleolus (tendons, artery, vein, nerve, FHL).
transversus abdominis: Lower 6 costal cartilages, thoracolumbar fascia, iliac crest, inguinal ligament
Lower intercostal nerves T7–11, subcostal T12, iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal L1
Compresses abdominal contents; raises intra-abdominal pressure
Deepest abdominal wall muscle; forms the conjoint tendon.
quadratus lumborum: 12th rib and transverse processes of L1–4
Lateral flexion of trunk; fixes the 12th rib
Lies behind the kidney in the posterior abdominal wall.
external intercostal muscles: Fibres run downward and forward ("hands in pockets").
internal intercostal muscles: Fibres run downward and backward at right angles to the externals.
pubococcygeus: Nerve to levator ani (S3–4) and perineal branch of pudendal
Supports pelvic organs; part of levator ani
Injury in childbirth contributes to prolapse and incontinence.
masseter: Lateral ramus and angle of mandible
Powerful jaw elevator; the parotid duct crosses it.
temporalis: Coronoid process and anterior ramus of mandible
Used to test V3: clench teeth and palpate.
medial pterygoid: Medial surface of lateral pterygoid plate; tuber of maxilla
Medial surface of angle of mandible
Elevates mandible and helps side-to-side chewing
Forms a muscular sling with masseter.
lateral pterygoid: Upper head: greater wing of sphenoid. Lower head: lateral pterygoid plate
Pterygoid fovea of mandible and TMJ disc
Lateral lowers, the rest lift: it is the only masticatory muscle that opens the mouth.
zygomaticus major: Facial nerve (VII), zygomatic and buccal branches
Facial palsy flattens the smile on that side.
bucinator: Parotid duct pierces it; supplied by VII, not V (sensory nerve is V3).
frontalis: Forehead is spared in an upper motor neuron facial palsy (bilateral cortical supply).
genioglossus: Tongue deviates toward the weak side in XII palsy; keeps the airway open.
lateral rectus: LR6 SO4 AO3: abducens, trochlear, oculomotor for the rest.
superior oblique: Trochlear nerve is the only cranial nerve to exit the dorsal brainstem and its nucleus supplies the opposite eye.
levator palpebrae superioris: Upper eyelid tarsal plate and skin
Oculomotor nerve (III) plus sympathetic to superior tarsal part
Ptosis occurs in III palsy (complete) and Horner syndrome (partial).
scalenus anterior: Anterior tubercles of C3–6 transverse processes
Phrenic nerve lies on its front; subclavian vein in front and artery/brachial plexus behind (scalene triangle).
posterior crico-arytenoid: The only abductor of the vocal cords: its paralysis is dangerous in bilateral injury.
straight part of cricothyroid: External laryngeal nerve (superior laryngeal branch of vagus)
Only intrinsic laryngeal muscle not supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
anterior belly of digastric: Posterior belly is supplied by the facial nerve.
palmar interossei muscles: Extensor expansions of the same fingers
PAD and DAB: Palmar ADduct, Dorsal ABduct.

median nerve: Roots C5–T1; formed from lateral and medial cords. Supplies most forearm flexors and the thenar muscles + lateral 2 lumbricals (LOAF).
Carpal tunnel syndrome; ape hand and "hand of benediction" in higher lesions.
ulnar nerve: Roots C8–T1 from the medial cord. Passes behind the medial epicondyle. Supplies FCU, medial FDP, most intrinsic hand muscles.
Claw hand; Froment's sign; "funny bone" injury at the elbow.
radial nerve: Roots C5–T1 from the posterior cord. Spirals in the radial groove. Supplies all extensors of arm and forearm.
Wrist drop after mid-shaft humeral fracture or Saturday night palsy.
axillary nerve: Roots C5–6 from the posterior cord. Winds round the surgical neck. Supplies deltoid and teres minor.
Anterior shoulder dislocation or surgical neck fracture; numb badge patch.
sciatic nerve: Roots L4–S3, largest nerve. Leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen below piriformis, splits into tibial and common fibular nerves.
Give gluteal IM injections in the upper outer quadrant to avoid it.
femoral nerve: Roots L2–4. Passes under the inguinal ligament lateral to the femoral artery. Supplies quadriceps, sartorius, pectineus.
Weak knee extension; loss of knee jerk; saphenous branch is cutaneous to medial leg.
tibial nerve: Roots L4–S3. Descends the posterior leg, passes behind the medial malleolus (tarsal tunnel), divides into medial and lateral plantar nerves.
Tarsal tunnel syndrome; cannot plantarflex or invert.
vagus nerve: Cranial nerve X: parasympathetic to thorax and most of the gut, motor to pharynx and larynx. Right recurrent laryngeal loops around the subclavian artery; left loops around the aortic arch.
Hoarse voice after thyroid or aortic surgery; uvula deviates away from a lesion.
facial nerve: Cranial nerve VII: leaves the skull by the stylomastoid foramen, crosses the parotid; supplies facial muscles, anterior 2/3 taste, lacrimal and salivary glands.
Bell's palsy (LMN): whole side of face weak. UMN lesion spares the forehead.
trigeminal nerve: Cranial nerve V: V1 ophthalmic, V2 maxillary, V3 mandibular. Sensory to face, motor to muscles of mastication (V3).
Trigeminal neuralgia: lancinating pain in V2/V3; corneal reflex uses V1.
oculomotor nerve: Cranial nerve III: supplies four extraocular muscles, levator palpebrae and parasympathetic to pupil constrictor and ciliary muscle.
Complete palsy: eye down and out, ptosis, dilated pupil. Compressed first by posterior communicating aneurysm.
brachial plexus: Roots C5–T1 → trunks (upper, middle, lower) → divisions → cords (lateral, posterior, medial) → branches. Mnemonic: Randy Travis Drinks Cold Beer.
Erb–Duchenne palsy (C5–6) waiter's tip; Klumpke (C8–T1) claw hand.
abdominal aorta: Starts at aortic hiatus (T12), ends at bifurcation L4 into common iliac arteries.
Aneurysm risk; palpable midline above the umbilicus.
ascending aorta: Begins at aortic valve; gives right and left coronary arteries from the sinuses of Valsalva.
Aortic dissection: tearing pain; Stanford type A involves it.
thoracic aorta: Descends from T4 to the aortic hiatus at T12 in the posterior mediastinum.
Gives the posterior intercostal arteries; coarctation lies near the ligamentum arteriosum.
femoral artery: Continuation of external iliac at inguinal ligament; femoral pulse at the mid-inguinal point. Divides into profunda femoris and superficial femoral.
Access site for angiography; femoral hernia lies medial to the vein.
radial artery: Branch of brachial artery at the cubital fossa; pulse lies lateral to flexor carpi radialis.
Used for arterial blood gas; Allen test checks palmar arch.
common carotid artery: Right arises from brachiocephalic; left from aortic arch. Divides at C4 (upper border of thyroid cartilage).
Carotid sinus at the bifurcation senses pressure; carotid massage can cause bradycardia.
internal carotid artery: Ascends to the skull with no branches in the neck, enters through the carotid canal, supplies brain and eye.
Atherosclerotic stenosis causes TIA and amaurosis fugax.
external carotid artery: Has 8 branches in the neck/face (superior thyroid, ascending pharyngeal, lingual, facial, occipital, posterior auricular, maxillary, superficial temporal).
Ends in the parotid; middle meningeal artery arises from the maxillary branch.
right coronary artery: Arises from the right aortic sinus; supplies right atrium and ventricle, SA node (≈60%), AV node (≈80%); gives posterior descending artery in right-dominant hearts.
Occlusion gives inferior MI and may cause bradycardia/AV block.
left coronary artery: Arises from the left aortic sinus; divides into LAD (anterior interventricular) and circumflex.
LAD occlusion is the "widow-maker" anterior MI.
hepatic portal vein: Formed behind the neck of the pancreas by the superior mesenteric and splenic veins; carries nutrient-rich blood to the liver.
Portal hypertension opens porto-systemic anastomoses: oesophageal varices, caput medusae, haemorrhoids.
inferior vena cava: Formed by common iliac veins at L5; passes through the diaphragm at T8 and enters the right atrium.
Tumour or clot can spread along it; IVC filters prevent PE.
superior vena cava: Formed by the brachiocephalic veins behind the 1st right costal cartilage; drains head, neck, upper limbs into right atrium.
SVC syndrome: facial swelling and distended neck veins (often lung cancer).
humerus: Long bone of the arm with head, surgical and anatomical necks, radial groove, epicondyles, capitulum and trochlea.
Surgical neck → axillary nerve; shaft → radial nerve; supracondylar → brachial artery and median nerve.
clavicle: S-shaped bone connecting upper limb to axial skeleton; ossifies first (intramembranous) and last to fuse.
Most commonly fractured bone; breaks at junction of middle and lateral thirds, medial fragment pulled up by SCM.
scaphoid bone: Largest bone of the proximal carpal row; forms the floor of the anatomical snuffbox.
Fracture after a fall on an outstretched hand; proximal pole may undergo avascular necrosis; tender snuffbox, often invisible on early X-ray.
femur: Longest, strongest bone; head, neck, greater and lesser trochanters, linea aspera, condyles.
Neck of femur fracture in the elderly risks avascular necrosis of the head (medial circumflex femoral artery).
radius: Lateral forearm bone; head, tuberosity, styloid process, Lister's tubercle.
Colles' fracture: distal radius, dorsally displaced, "dinner fork" deformity.
sacrum: Five fused vertebrae forming the posterior pelvis; sacral promontory, four pairs of foramina.
Sacral hiatus is used for caudal epidural; sacral promontory is an obstetric landmark.
mandible: Only mobile skull bone; body, ramus, angle, condyle, coronoid process, mental foramen.
Fractures are often bilateral; inferior alveolar nerve may be injured.
